speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: A new WSH Framework was launched in 2005 following the occurrence of several major workplace accidents, including the Nicoll Highway collapse in 2004.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under this framework, the regulatory regime was strengthened through the enactment of the Workplace Safety and Health Act (WSH Act) in 2006.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We stepped up efforts to work with industry and the tripartite partners to develop WSH capabilities and raise WSH awareness on the importance of safety and health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Our WSH 2018 target is now within reach, but we cannot be complacent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: I have said it many times but I think it bears repeating, that is, every life lost is just one too many.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We must, therefore, redouble our efforts to entrench the right WSH mindset, eradicate unsafe and unhealthy work practices and enhance WSH capabilities to create safe and healthy workplaces for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Our WSH journey over the last decade has taught us that all workplace injuries and ill-health are preventable with the full commitment of every stakeholder, that is, employers, workers, unions and the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We need a stronger emphasis on preventing harm from ever occurring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Prevention is, therefore, key to achieving safe and healthy workplaces for everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: There are three areas where we can strengthen the culture of prevention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, we need to prevent the occurrence of unsafe work practices and health risks at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, should an accident happen, we need to prevent its recurrence, especially for accidents that are complex, involving risks that are not well-understood and have the potential for serious harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Third, we need to prevent workplace safety and health training courses from becoming outdated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, on preventing occurrence of unsafe work practices and health risks at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: When the WSH Act was enacted to replace the then-Factories Act in 2006, the penalty framework to deal with offenders was significantly enhanced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The maximum fine was raised by 2.5 times from $200,000 to $500,000 under the WSH Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In cases where it is a repeated offence resulting in death, the maximum fine for corporate offenders can go up to $1 million.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Last year, the High Court laid out a framework to guide sentencing for WSH Act offences that took into account the level of culpability, severity and potential harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The State Courts have since imposed higher penalties in prosecutions under the WSH Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The higher penalties under the WSH Act have played a part in underscoring the seriousness of WSH offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, these penalties have mostly been applied to WSH offences when serious harm has already occurred.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: While we can penalise the companies, it is already too late for the injured or deceased workers and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Prevention is still the better option to protect against unnecessary loss of lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To strengthen the culture of prevention, we need to send a stronger signal that unsafe work practices and exposure to health risks are unacceptable, even when there are no accidents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Through our inspections, we uncover a wide spectrum of WSH offences every year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For minor offences that are unlikely to cause harm, we issue warnings and require rectification of the WSH lapses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, there have been instances where no harm has occurred, but the companies have shown disregard for basic safety and health requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If we had not discovered them during our inspections, it would be a matter of time before they result in serious harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For example, during one of our routine inspections last year, we found a worksite with multiple open sides in different locations close to where the workers were deployed, therefore, exposing workers to risk of falling from height.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: There were also other lapses, such as electrical hazards and tripping risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These were serious accidents waiting to happen and were averted only by sheer luck.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Currently, we issue composition fines and Stop Work Orders for such serious cases of offenders where no harm has occurred.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, we have seen a doubling of such cases, from 13 in 2013 to 26 in 2016.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We need to take a tougher deterrent stance and prosecute them under the WSH Act subsidiary legislation (SL), including first-time egregious offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For the SL prosecution to have effective deterrent value, the SL penalties should also be increased.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is consistent with the 2.5 times increase in the maximum penalty under the WSH Act, from $200,000 to $500,000 which was enacted in 2006.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will apply the $50,000 maximum fine to SL offences that may cause or result in death, serious injury or dangerous occurrence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: They account for about 80% of all SL offences now, mostly with a maximum fine of $20,000.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Some of these offences include failure to have protective structures, such as barriers at open sides or around excavations, to prevent falls, and failure to appoint authorised persons to supervise hazardous works, thereby exposing workers to danger that may result in death or serious injury.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Even as we raise the maximum fine under SL for the majority of the offences, the penalties we seek will be calibrated based on factors, such as the culpability of the offender, the severity of harm that could have resulted, and the likelihood of harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will only prosecute the more egregious cases where the offenders have ignored the safety and health of workers and serious harm is likely to occur.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, to prevent recurrence of complex accidents, where the risks are not well-understood and have the potential for serious harm and could be present in other companies, we need to ensure timely sharing of learnings from the investigation into such accidents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The learnings are needed not just to raise awareness of safety and health risks, but to provide recommendations on how to eliminate or mitigate the risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Currently, case facts of complex accidents are released only after the conclusion of criminal proceedings, which could take around three years from the time of accident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is done so as not to prejudice the outcome of legal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, the learning value to industry is delayed, and the risk of such an accident recurring persists for a longer period of time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We believe timely and early sharing of case facts and recommendations with the industry is important to prevent recurrence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Learning reports will not be released for all accidents, but only where the Commissioner for WSH considers it to be necessary in the interest of the public, particularly for those where the risks were not so well-understood and have the potential for serious harm and could be present in other companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The learning report is not intended to apportion blame or liability, but simply to allow other companies to learn from the accident and take immediate steps to avoid similar circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The learning report will only contain information necessary for learning value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We do not intend to name companies or individuals, and there will be no statements of liability in the report.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To further allay industry concerns over unwarranted reputational damage or unintended disclosure of intellectual property, we will establish a process to consult relevant parties on the draft report before publishing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Allowing the release of information for the sole purpose of learning without attributing blame or liability is not new and has been adopted in other situations and countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For example, investigation reports by the Transport Safety Investigation Bureau under the Ministry of Transport (MOT) are published for the sole purpose of accident prevention, and their reports are also inadmissible in any civil or criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The United States (US) Chemical Safety Board (CSB) and the United Kingdom (UK) Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) also release accident investigation reports focused solely on improving safety and not to apportion blame or liability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Accident investigation reports by CSB and RAIB may also be issued, whether or not civil or criminal proceedings are in progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These reports and lessons learnt have enhanced the industry's understanding of specific areas of risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Many of these safety recommendations by CSB and RAIB have been implemented by the industry, resulting in safer chemical facilities, safer transport and safer communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To sustain improvement in our WSH performance, a workforce competent and skilled in managing WSH is critical.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Over the years, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has worked with the industry to define standards and guide the design of WSH-related courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As the industries undergo transformations to create new and better jobs, we need to ensure that WSH courses remain up to date with the latest content and training methods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As part of this effort, we have been working very closely with SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and the WSH training industry to align the current WSH courses to the national Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) system and transfer the accreditation of WSH training providers to SSG.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under the SSG accreditation system, training providers are not only required to ensure that their training content is relevant to the industry, but also that their teaching methods are up to date.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For example, training providers are expected to leverage technologies, such as Virtual Reality, and use innovative learning approaches to enhance the quality and the effectiveness of learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This helps to make learning more engaging and will also lead to better WSH learning outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With SSG being the single authority to accredit all WSH training providers by 2019, clauses 4 and 5 are consequential amendments to remove the requirement for the Commissioner to accredit WSH training providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Currently, the personal liability protection for inspectors under the WSH Act is limited to equipment damages due to a prescribed examination or test, and the Commissioner's and Deputy Commissioner's duties in relation to a remedial order or stop-work order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is similar to the personal liability protection provision under other legislation, such as the Fire Safety Act and the Environmental Protection and Management Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to reassure the House that protection will only be extended to inspectors and authorised officers who have exercised reasonable care and consideration in the execution of their duties under the WSH Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Countries, including Germany and the UK, which have put together greater emphasis to entrench a culture of prevention, have already achieved this lower fatality rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: There is much that we can learn from these countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Enacting progressive WSH legislation is necessary but insufficient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Collectively, we will identify WSH challenges ahead, chart directions and develop key strategies to make Singapore one of the safest and healthiest workplaces in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will be a very big challenge but, together with our tripartite partners and industry stakeholders, I believe we will be able to achieve it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: On this note, I humbly ask all Members of this House for their support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: She was a new mom to a six-month-old daughter.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was her first week back at work from maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: She was working in the laboratory when the explosion occurred.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Tragically, the emergency response team was unable to locate her and her remains were only discovered after firefighters had put out the fire.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The incident hit close to home as the victim was one of our members in the Chemical Industries Employees' Union (CIEU).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On that fateful day, a husband lost his wife, a child her mother, the parents their daughter.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Seven other employees were also injured in the fire, suffering from lacerations, burns and smoke inhalation injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We would never wish this upon anyone and the lessons learnt there are just as pertinent today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The WSH Act was enacted in 2006 for the very purpose of preventing such incidents from occurring and is structured based on three key principles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, reducing risks at source; second, engendering industry ownership of WSH outcomes; and third, preventing workplace accidents through higher penalties for poor safety management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The review of the Act is, therefore, timely as we seek to further enhance workplace safety at our various workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am supportive of the intent behind the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I have a few questions to seek clarification on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The higher maximum fine is intended for offences which could result in death, serious bodily injury or dangerous occurrence even where harm has not occurred yet.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While I agree with the intent of this amendment, I would like to seek clarity from the Minister as to what offences would the increased maximum fine apply to, and to request the Minister to share some examples of incidents where such heightened penalties are required.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, the Bill provides for the sharing of learning reports with findings on major incidents so that the industry can take corrective steps as soon as possible to prevent complex and major accidents from recurring.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is provided in the Bill that such a learning report would not be admissible as evidence in any civil, criminal, arbitral or disciplinary proceedings before any Court, tribunal or body or proceedings under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I see the value of sharing learning expeditiously to prevent recurrence of the accident.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I have concerns if there are sufficient safeguards in place to ensure that investigations and due process will not be prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, have five questions on this proposed amendment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, I would like to ask the Minister if these learning reports would be made available to the public and on what platforms would these reports be shared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, what types of incidents would qualify as a complex and major accident which requires the publishing of this learning report?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, I would like to ask the Minister what safeguards are in place to ensure that these learning reports will not prejudice the outcomes of subsequent civil or criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the reports are not admissible as evidence in legal proceedings, the reports may result in preconceived positions or biases in witnesses, and public discussion of these reports may also invariably cause impressions to be formed which may affect the outcome of the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, I am concerned that companies, in conducting their internal review of accidents, may rely on these learning reports to take premature action to discipline or dismiss their employees before official investigations are completed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, in the tragic train track accident last year, which took the lives of two SMRT trainees, SMRT fired two staff following their internal review of the accident before official investigations were concluded.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The union's position is that it is important to allow due process to take its course and for all facts to be revealed through official investigations before drawing any conclusions which impact the livelihood of workers involved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, I would like to ask the Minister what safeguards are in place to ensure that these learning reports will not prejudice the outcomes of official investigations by MOM or the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and other relevant agencies, and to what extent the content in these learning reports would differ from the reports from these official investigations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The last amendment which I would like to address is the removal of the requirement for the Commissioner to accredit WSH training as MOM transfers the accreditation of training to SSG.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I agree that having accreditation functions under SSG will enable SSG to have a more holistic view of adult education and training and undertake a more coordinated approach towards audits and quality assurance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), the WSH Secretariat works with the network of 58 affiliated unions on improving WSH conditions of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The secretariat also works with trade associations and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to reach out to workers to raise awareness of the importance of WSH.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Singapore Institute of Safety Officers (SISO) is also one of the Labour Movement's U Associate partners in developing WSH professionals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge SSG and the training providers to work closely with the Labour Movement to raise the standards of WSH training and mobilise more of our working people to adopt safer practices at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, training providers should leverage technology to ensure greater accessibility to training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This can be done through bite-size modular training which can be completed on the go, such as through e-learning modules, and leverage technology, such as virtual reality, to help learners pick up safety concepts in a safe yet realistic environment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, NTUC Learning Hub is looking into training which adopts virtual reality and augmented reality for work-at-heights courses and courses which are scenario-specific to the workers' work environment, for example, shipyards and construction sites.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These scenarios can then be easily modified to test the trainees in different environments with varied levels of risk assessment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   This amendment Bill has made improvements in the following three areas to ensure that workplace safety will be more enhanced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The employers and the workers must work together to build a safer workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While we prepare the learning report, safeguards must be in place to ensure that it does not interfere with the investigation of the case.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The report will also help us to learn lessons and nip potential accidents in the bud.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope that SSG will work with the industry associations, unions, employers and employees on training curriculum and standards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): At the end of the day, top-down enforcement and enhancing legislation can only go so far.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Everyone along the value chain has a part to play.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Leaders of organisations need to take ownership of safety as a core business value.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Supervisors need to lead by example and workers on the ground cannot be complacent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must be proactive in ensuring that our work environment is safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the viaduct at the Pan-Island Expressway worksite at Upper Changi Road East collapsed and killed a worker and injured 10 others in July, Singaporeans were shocked and saddened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though many of the workers who are most exposed to the risk of injuries at the workplace are foreign workers, Singaporeans do not discriminate but instead feel for them as fellow workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a common humanity in seeing bodies broken by preventable accidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are no national differences in knowing families are devastated by the lives of loved ones lost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As far as this Bill seeks to achieve the goals of the WSH 2018 Plus strategy, it is a commendable move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the new WSH framework was implemented in 2005, workplace injuries and fatalities have come down substantially.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is scope to go down further, as many advanced industrial countries, such as the UK, Sweden, Germany and the Netherlands, have lower rates, as low as 1.0.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the four strategic outcomes for WSH 2018 is for Singapore to be renowned as a centre of excellence for WSH.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I am glad that Minister of State Sam Tan had mentioned that we will be competing with these leaders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We seem to have hit a roadblock in improving WSH.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To tackle the roadblock, WSH 2018 Plus seeks to adopt a differentiated enforcement approach to improve the WSH performance of companies with different capabilities and attitudes, and to build collective ownership of a pervasive WSH culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This suggests that the roadblock appears to be a widespread organisational culture that goes against WSH principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I say this without being facetious in reference to the SMRT saga.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister confirm that this is a problem that we are now facing with regard to WSH progress?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is so, then the amendments in this Bill to give the Commissioner the power to prepare and publish a learning report on any accident, dangerous occurrence or occupational disease in a workplace under investigation should be supported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the first point I would like to bring up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to create a positive learning culture of respect and concern for the well-being of our workers rather than a culture of blame, scapegoating and compensation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this light, that the learning report is inadmissible as evidence in Court proceedings and that an inspector involved in the learning report cannot be compelled to give testimony or evidence, are understandable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is an Inquiry Committee that the Minister can appoint under the WSH Act to hold an inquiry into any accident, dangerous occurrence or occupational disease, which could lead to criminal proceedings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second is an inquiry under the Coroners Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third is an inquiry by a commission of inquiry or a committee of inquiry under the Inquiries Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This adds layers of complexity that may affect the preparation and publication of a learning report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the Commissioner becomes aware of an accident in a workplace, he or she may direct an inspector to investigate the accident.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Depending on the findings of the investigation, he may direct a learning report to be prepared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Commissioner may also recommend to the Minister to appoint an Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, how can the inspector be expected to not compromise the objectives of the learning report, knowing that the report will be admitted as evidence for the Inquiry Committee and he can be compelled to testify before it?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Inquiry Committee recommends criminal proceedings to be instituted by submitting a copy of the report to the Public Prosecutor, then in the subsequent criminal proceedings, can the learning report be admitted as evidence and the inspector called to testify before the Court?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is some ambiguity as to whether section 27B(1) and (2) allow for this subsequent development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moving on to my second point, we need to better tackle occupational diseases and improve workplace health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond the headline-grabbing accidents, MOM statistics for the recent years show that the number of confirmed occupational diseases is rising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the occupational diseases and workplace health issues are less visible and their impact less immediate, because they have what is called a long latency period, some diseases taking many years to surface after exposure to the causes, they can have far greater life-changing impact on workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The WSH strategy is currently oriented towards reducing workplace fatality and injury.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe there is a need to pay equal attention to occupational diseases and workplace health, with appropriate targets in reducing incidences of occupational diseases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is in this arena that I think a positive learning culture would have multiplier effects on improving workplace health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the learning report is not so useful in this respect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The learning report instrument is useful for workplace safety, as learning points could be quickly shared and corrections quickly made to prevent similar accidents from happening across an industrial sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This instrument is less useful for workplace health, as the long latency period of occupational diseases could mean that thousands of workers would have been affected by the time an incidence is made known and a learning report published.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a need for a different model here due to the different nature of occupational diseases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The learning report model is also less useful because many of our workers exposed to occupational diseases are foreign workers and the long latency period of occupational diseases means that these workers may only develop ill-health after they have gone home or are sent back because of their ill-health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Incidences of occupational disease will go unreported in such cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could learn from the UK government’s Health and Safety Executive (HSE), the counterpart of our WSH Council (WSHC).

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two aspects we can learn from and to adapt for our efforts to tackle occupation diseases and workplace health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because these potentially affect many workers and were shown to have high incidence of disease.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One issue that will subvert any model is under-reporting of accidents and occupational diseases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is my third and last point: we need to tackle the under-reporting of accidents to make the learning report instrument effective and to make ownership of a learning WSH culture possible and meaningful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there under-reporting of accidents and occupational diseases here in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are some indications there could be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Non-government organisations, such as Transient Workers Count Too, have raised this concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, the Government’s approach to occupational diseases is more stringent and progressive, as doctors are required to report any of the occupational diseases listed in the Second Schedule of the WSH Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is conveniently done through MOM’s electronic notification system or the Ministry of Health's (MOH’s) Health Professional Portal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the WSHC’s Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Management of Occupational Diseases state on this reporting requirement, "A robust notification system provides important data for understanding the extent and depth of the occupational safety and health status in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps the authorities to identify persons and industries at risk, as well as to identify new and emerging ones." I think this is very well-said.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is required for employers, but they have no natural incentive to do this, especially when the injured workers are foreign workers who are not aware of their rights or are too afraid of having their employment terminated by their employers and forcibly repatriated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Doctors are better placed to report the injuries as suspected to be resulting from workplace accidents since they are pledged to a professional ethical code and have the knowledge to give a proper diagnosis of the injuries and opinion as to the causes of the injuries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the system is already in place for doctors to report occupational diseases in a convenient and accessible manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is very little cost to adding on the requirement for doctors to report injuries due to suspected workplace accidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps the authorities to identify persons and industries at risk, as well as to identify new and emerging ones." This applies equally to workplace accidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As with the learning report instrument, such reporting does not have to end in blame and liability, but in getting the whole industry sectors to take responsibility and ownership of WSH.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot see the logic of excluding required reporting by doctors of injuries in this new learning culture we are trying to promote.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It should be engrained in the DNAs of the organisation for us to achieve our vision towards zero accident.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our working people need to have a safe environment, as well as good health, to do their daily work efficiently and contribute at their optimum capacity.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Safety and health can affect an individual’s and a company’s productivity and, hence, influence the economic output of the company and the country as a whole.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is vital to strengthen industry ownership of WSH outcomes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Workplace incidents vary across industries and, hence, there should be more platforms for industries to come together at the sector level and share incidents and learning point for everyone to better understand the issues.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, we need to have a clear purpose and measurable outcomes to see if this initiative translates into intended outcomes on enhancing workplace safety.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should be clear links between such practices leading to a reduction in workplace incidents at the sectorial level.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, it is essential for all stakeholders to understand that such report sharing should not be a finger-pointing exercise where stakeholders may form a preconceived notion of the cause of the incident even before the investigation is conclusive, instead of using such case sharing to learn and to avoid similar incidents from occurring.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, besides penalties, there should also be rewards to motivate organisations and individuals to practise WSH as a way of life and as a DNA of its organisation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Penalty can be in the form of added tax.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Incentive can be in the form of tax rebates.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employers can then plough back this amount to institute additional safety measures or health programmes for employees, including for their mental health well-being.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to raise a dire concern of workplace abuse and harassment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Even though the Protection from Harassment Act provides an avenue for individuals to take civil or criminal action against perpetrators, there is still the hovering concern that such post-incident penalty does not reduce the number of such incidences over time and neither does it provide impetus for employers to put in place the required awareness, knowledge and training element, as well as preventive or deterrent measures, to protect employees from such abuses and harassment at the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Different employers have different levels of measures implemented, and some have none at the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Besides, such incidences not only affect the physical but also the psychological and emotional state of individuals if it happens.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can WICA include such forms of inflicting injury caused by abuse and harassment that are proven with evidence, instead of individuals taking up a costly civil case against perpetrators?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can there also be punitive action taken against employers who do not have processes or measures in place to protect employees from such abuses or do not act on clear alarm raised with due diligence?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With an increasing number of abuses and harassment over time, it is important that more needs to be done in this aspect.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Call it education awareness or mindset change, but nothing beats legislation and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Good working conditions are vital to helping workers feel safe, which will improve productivity and the competitiveness of our industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Any workplace fatality is one too many, and there can never be enough emphasis on ensuring that our workers, regardless of industry, have a safe working environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Achieving this will take a tremendous amount of effort and teamwork from all stakeholders, and the proposed amendments in this Bill would certainly serve as a good start.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A harsher deterrence will compel companies to sit up and take notice of the severity of a WSH offence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the enhanced penalties will serve to "incentivise" companies to focus on preventing workplace accidents rather than taking remedial actions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To foster an ideal WSH culture, the Ministry can consider adopting the Labour Movement’s 3Cs approach to improving the WSH awareness culture.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One, focus on better coordination by convincing companies to cut internal red tape, so as to enable smooth implementation of WSH initiatives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two, secure greater commitment across all levels in a company, from the top management to the ground supervisors, right down to general workers, to collectively commit to raising safety and health standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Three, engage in targeted coaching by having industry-specific WSH training courses or modules as part of the WSH accreditation process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to seek some clarifications on the provisions of the Bill which would allow the WSH Commissioner to make public a detailed incident learning report of any WSH incident while the incident is still under investigation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I can understand the intention to share learning points to plug potential safety gaps in companies working in the same industry, we need to be mindful of prejudicing the investigation results and stirring public opinion needlessly when findings have yet to be finalised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such reports can also be sensitive if a public-listed company is involved.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Premature release of information before prosecution may affect the share price, the company's business and, consequently, may affect workers and cause workers to be displaced or retrenched.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recently, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in the US had asked employers to submit detailed injury and illness logs to the agency for public posting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, industry groups are now suing OSHA, citing that the new rule exposes a business to significant reputational harm without proving that this has effectively reduced workplace injuries and illnesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is similar to the aviation industry, where an advisory can be first published and shared internally within industry players, followed by a detailed incident report later on.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am, therefore, assured to hear from the Minister of State that the Ministry will be judicious in the release of such learning reports.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Finland and Sweden have had workplace fatality rates of below 1.0 per 100,000 workers, and there are many lessons that we can learn from them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, Finland, which has about the same population as Singapore, has around 60,000 Occupational Safety and Health specialists, or about one for every 10 regular workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to propose for the Ministry to consider establishing a national register of trained WSH specialists.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would certainly help to facilitate the quick and effective dissemination of important WSH advisories to the ground.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, best practices can also be shared within specific industrial cluster in a prompt manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A central training centre, with the support of our tripartite partners, would also go a long way in grooming the next generation of WSH specialists and ensure proper progression within the sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The centre can also be given the mandate to come up with a customised Professional Conversion Programme and a Progressive Wage Model for safety officers to upskill and progress in their careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A clearly defined career path, with commensurate wages, will also help attract more local talents to the profession.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At this year’s Committee of Supply debate, I highlighted the need for a support framework, beyond the existing Workplace Injury Compensation Act, to help injured workers return to work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, the reality is that not many employers proactively help their injured employees during and after the rehabilitation process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I called for MOM to establish a scheme to better help injured workers – one which includes a structured case management system to help our workers with injury management, rehabilitation, job redesign and even job placement where necessary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I am happy to note that there are already companies which have appointed their own in-house RTW coordinators, such as Sembawang Shipyard.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the RTW programme in place, we now need to ask ourselves, what more can we do for injured workers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Australia, the US and the European Union (EU), the RTW framework is legislated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My final point, Mr Speaker, is that much of our WSH efforts today focus on workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A build-up of stress and fatigue can lead to distractions, which will place our workers at higher risk of getting injured at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, it is of paramount importance for us to practice WSH holistically, by focusing on the body, mind and soul, in order for our workplaces to be truly a safe and healthy environment for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the spectre of major incidents, such as the Pan-Island Expressway (PIE) worksite collapse, might linger, we are in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continue working towards ever safer workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When it comes to ensuring workplace safety, two key areas come to mind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: All workplace injuries and health issues are preventable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, it must be the goal of all companies to have zero accidents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A desire for zero fatalities and accidents would not just rest with the leaders of a company but it should be a collective aspiration that is shared with all workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A secure and accessible feedback mechanism should be in place for workers, especially in the construction, marine and engineering sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There should be a balancing or rebalancing of powers where workers and employers are concerned, as many workers, especially foreign workers, might feel afraid to speak up even if they know there are violations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What incentives are there for workers to be a whistleblower where safety is concerned?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What reassurance will they have and how will this be communicated to workers to encourage them to speak up?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is because, as part of the migration of WSH training courses from MOM to SkillsFuture SG, the training providers will have to go through re-accreditation to meet the new standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to MOM, it has been working with SSG to prepare the WSH training providers for this change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Minister of State provide an update on what percentage of companies have successfully made the migration and how many more are left to complete it by 2019?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the measures taken to ensure training capacity has not been affected?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will this incur higher costs for businesses and what are MOM’s plans to help them?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology is also a great enabler in some sectors as it can help reduce human error and accidents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Minister also share the progress of some examples of companies that have successfully used technology to enhance the safety processes at work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry also incentivise the adoption of technologies to reduce the occurrence of workplace accidents?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The progress towards safer workplaces is never a smooth or linear one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will be littered with unfortunate incidents that we must do well to learn from and better protect our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill will build on our previous efforts and is in the correct direction.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.56 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To achieve this bold ambition, our legislative and regulatory framework must identify and address the key causes of workplace accidents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The WSH 2018 Plus workplan had highlighted improving WSH performance in the construction industry as a key priority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the outset, it is necessary to recognise the reality that low-wage migrant workers form the bulk of the workforce in the construction industry and other sectors, such as marine and manufacturing, that are the top contributors of workplace fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: WSH laws can only be truly effective if they take into account the working realities of this group of workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have one clarification on the Bill and would like to further raise some points for consideration in the implementation of the WSH legislation and regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While occupational diseases may take a longer time to manifest, may be harder to detect and link causally to the workplace, their effects on the health of workers can be just as detrimental.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Part IV of the current Act on the duties of persons and Part VI on investigation powers do not distinguish between accidents and occupational diseases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the enhanced fines do not apply to breaches of regulations that may or actually lead to occupational diseases, can the Minister clarify why the distinction was drawn?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that workers have reported instances of employers with advance knowledge that an inspection was going to take place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that it is, indeed, the case that inspections are conducted without prior notice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or is it the case that there are announced inspections and unannounced inspections?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, what percentage of inspections is unannounced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, it is the duty of the employer under section 12(1) of the Bill to take practicable measures to ensure the safety and health of his employees at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the employer is not permitted under section 18(1) to deduct any sums for anything done or provided by him as part of such measures, civil society organisations have heard accounts from workers who were injured because they were not provided with, could not afford to buy, or could not afford to replace damaged safety equipment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, many workers report having to pay for safety equipment through salary deductions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, can the Minister clarify if it is within the scope of safety inspections to ensure that employers are not deducting costs for safety equipment from workers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a relevant contributing factor to workers not having the necessary equipment for their health and safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, section 16 of the Bill requires manufacturers and suppliers of machinery, equipment or hazardous substance to provide information about precaution, hazards and safe use.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such information may not be provided in a language that is understood by the foreign workers who form the bulk of the workforce most vulnerable to workplace hazards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm if it is the responsibility of employers and principals to ensure that workers understand the written safety advice and instruction provided by manufacturers and suppliers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fifth, the WSH Guidelines note that fatigue can lead to physical and mental impairment, which increases error rates and risk of injuries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such fatigue can accumulate as a result of workers being required to perform overtime work day after day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Civil society organisations report encountering workers who work beyond the maximum allowable overtime hours, with little or no days off.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Tight schedules, budget, and man-year entitlement limitations might lead to workers being asked to work longer hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, despite MOM's extensive efforts in safety inspections, many workplace violations may still go unnoticed if not reported by workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, if reporting safety violations means that workers are likely to lose their jobs, workers are not going to be willing to come forward regardless of MOM's best attempts at encouraging reporting of safety violations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 18(2) prevents an employer from dismissing an employee who assists authorities where there have been breaches of health and safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employees are required to report such instances through the Employment Act appeal mechanisms for unfair dismissal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there may be insufficient protection for low-wage migrant workers who can have their Work Permits cancelled and repatriated, with no opportunity to challenge their termination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is MOM able to share the number of employees that have successfully appealed an unfair dismissal under section 18(2)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Providing employees with stronger whistleblower protection will encourage reporting of WSH Act violations from the stakeholders who have the best knowledge of such violations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that MOM will increase its collaborations with civil society groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the end of the day, of all the legislative changes, regulatory amendments and workplans, the goal should be to improve the outcomes for the workers on the ground.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This House that we are debating in, this very Chamber, was built by many foreign workers who come to Singapore in search of a better life for their own loved ones back in their own countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They come with hopes and aspirations, after having paid their agents exorbitant amounts of money or perhaps having sold off jewellery, ancestral land, just to get here, they slog day and night, forgoing days off and working countless hours of overtime, just to earn that little extra.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But when it all comes crashing down, their dreams die – theirs and their loved ones' as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The loss of a life is irreplaceable, whoever it may be.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Minister of State said in his opening statement, one is too many.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I welcome and support the changes proposed in the WSH amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Workplace safety is for all workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, stand fully behind the Ministry's decision to set up Total WSH Service Centres in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I hope that the pilot project at Woodlands would be successful in implementing WSH programmes for workers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If it takes off, we can look forward to more of such centres in industrial areas around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, returning to the case of foreign workers, I believe that they are also eligible for more training.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to ask the Ministry if the training provided for our foreign workers at their countries of origin is sufficient at the current moment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Does the Ministry know how successful the scheme has been and how many workers have benefited from this training?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Also, how many of them are still in Singapore, working in industries relevant to the training that they had received?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also wonder if the Ministry conducts aptitude tests for our registered foreign workers here in Singapore, especially those in the construction industry, to see if they have the right fit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These workers are hardworking, I have no doubt about it, but would it not be better if we could ascertain that they are also up to the task, both mentally and physically, as well as technically?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If they are prepared to voice concerns regarding safety at their workplaces, because they are adequately equipped with such information, it would make for a better and safer work environment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I am certain that many, in fear of preserving their own rice bowls, may muzzle their comments or feedback in fear of reprisals from their supervisors, managers or employers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If only a worker had voiced concerns about unsafe practices, many industrial accidents and loss of lives could have been prevented.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am suggesting that unsafe workplace practices have been carried out on different worksites, and perhaps with the knowledge of workers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the incident learning report, as required under this amendment to the Bill, would be a welcome one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I would like to hear the Ministry's views on this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, the UK, Sweden, the Netherlands and Finland have already achieved that target.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, we have a lot of catching up to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The integration of WSH training standards is laudable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry could advise if the transfer of accreditation to SSG is smooth at the current moment and if the numbers are on track.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Do the companies meet the requirements as set out by SSG and how many training providers are we looking at, at a steady state?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Families want assurances that their loved ones return home safe from work every day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The amendment Bill is a step in the right direction and, while I support the Bill, I would appreciate if the Ministry could address my concerns, as stated in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And while some of the suggestions I have made may lie outside the ambit of this current Bill, I hope that they will be considered under WSH 2028 for future amendments.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I will now address the specific issues that have been raised.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Melvin Yong asked for examples of accidents which will merit a learning report.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay was particularly concerned that a learning report may prejudice legal proceedings and Government investigations.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Both Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Thanaletchimi felt that a learning report may result in preconceived positions or biases in witnesses and the public.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Alex Yam asked if there is any conflict of interest between MOM's criminal investigation and the learning report.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This means accidents that are complex, where the risks are not well-understood and have the potential for serious harm.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In November 2013, a flash fire occurred in an incineration plant.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Three workers suffered burn injuries and the whole plant was razed almost to the ground.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Even nearby companies were affected by the fire.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: It was extremely fortunate that no one had died.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The flash fire was caused by the mixing of incompatible chemicals, a process also practised in other companies, but where the risks were not well-understood.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: During those 16 months, two incidents occurred in other companies that had similar processes.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: If companies had been more aware of the risks of incompatible chemical mixing, they would have taken preventive measures, by reviewing their testing procedures and installing detection equipment.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Fortunately, both were smaller scale incidents that did not result in serious harm, but they could have escalated into major incidents with dire consequences.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Therefore, it is essential in the public interest to share the detailed facts and lessons from such incidents as soon as possible, so that others can be more informed and their lives are protected.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Learning reports will, therefore, not prejudice such proceedings.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This includes disciplinary proceedings in companies, as cited by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Any company can conduct their own investigation and take disciplinary actions according to their own findings.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: However, any worker who considers that he has been unfairly dismissed can appeal to MOM.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Learning reports explain what factors caused the accident, such as incompatible chemical mixing.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: They do not pinpoint who was at fault or assign liability to the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked on the admissibility of the learning report in inquiries under the WSH Act and the Inquiries Act or the Coroners Act.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: For inquiries under the WSH Act and the Inquiries Act, separate learning reports will not be needed in those circumstances as the full and official inquiries would have been conducted by the Inquiry Committees.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: For inquiries under the Coroners Act, they are only to determine the cause of death or the identity of the deceased.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Under the Coroners Act, the inquiry shall not determine any question of criminal, civil or disciplinary liability.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In any case, any learning report admitted into evidence in a Coroner's Inquiry will not be admissible in any subsequent criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how learning reports will be disseminated, and Mr Melvin Yong suggested to share only with relevant industry players, as such releases may negatively affect businesses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will assess the extent of sharing for each learning report on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Where the report is relevant only for a particular group of companies, such as if the risks are due to specialised processes found only in these companies, we will share the report with the specific companies concerned.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Where the report can improve safety and health in many companies, we will share the report on the WSHC website for the wider public interest.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We believe the sharing of learning reports will help prevent further accidents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Any major accident will have implications on companies' reputation.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Weighing reputational cost against the cost of human lives, I think all of us will agree that the top priority must be to save lives.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Sharing learning reports should, therefore, outweigh other considerations.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, for companies, the best way to avoid reputational damage is to be serious in taking the necessary WSH measures to prevent accidents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Alex Yam asked if the increased penalty of fines of $50,000 sufficiently deters the loss of lives, while Mr Desmond Choo asked about the treatment of errant companies for public tenders.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Other than penalties under the WSH Act, errant companies can be placed into the Business Under Surveillance (BUS) programme, and are subjected to the Demerit Points System which restricts their access to foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Public agencies already take into account bidders' safety record, such as demerit points and BUS programme, in their procurement assessment.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Melvin Yong asked what offences under SL would be prescribed the increased $50,000 maximum fine.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if this will include offences leading to occupational diseases.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: In addition to the offences cited earlier, they would include failure to provide personal protective equipment for hazardous work, failure to implement a WSH management system or plans for safe work environment and procedures, failure to inspect critical equipment, such as cranes, scaffolds and formwork, as well as not ensuring workers have the necessary training for their role.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Offences that may result in occupational diseases, such as failure to effectively enclose asbestos work areas, or failure to take measures to protect workers from toxic dust, fumes or other contaminants will also be included.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Of the Approved Training Providers (ATPs) initially providing the 23 courses, 62%, or 41 of them, were successfully appointed under the WSQ Framework for WSH courses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Unsuccessful ATPs can still participate in future accreditation exercises, where appropriate, for the remaining 33 WSH courses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: So, those unsuccessful ATPs can still try to meet the criteria set by SSG on these remaining 33 courses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We encourage them to review their operations and delivery capabilities for the courses to meet SSG's accreditation framework.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: There was no disruption to training capacity due to the migration.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: SSG considers the ability of WSQ-accredited training providers to meet industry demand in the accreditation process.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: SSG will work with training providers to ramp up training capacity if needed.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: There was also no increase in WSH course fees to businesses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Melvin Yong asked how the quality of WSH curriculum and training content will be maintained under SSG, with MOM being the subject matter experts on WSH.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay also suggested that curriculum development should be done through close engagements with the industry associations and practitioners, unions and workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: I agree with their views and I am happy to report that this is, indeed, the approach taken for developing the WSH curriculum and its contents.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM and WSHC, where the tripartite partners are represented, will continue to be closely involved in the WSH training curriculum.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: As the national authority on WSH, MOM is partnering SSG in developing and incorporating updated WSH skills into the Skills Frameworks of relevant industries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Patrick Tay recommended that training providers leverage technology to ensure greater accessibility to training, such as virtual reality, to enable learning in a safe yet realistic environment.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Under SSG, training providers are encouraged to use innovative training approaches through technology.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Alex Yam asked if training centres set up in source countries sufficiently introduce foreign workers to basic construction techniques and also enquired on the retention rate for trained construction workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Since 2005, it has been mandatory for foreign construction workers to be trained at Overseas Testing Centres and to pass a basic skills evaluation test conducted by Building and Construction Authority (BCA) officers before they can start working in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The testing by BCA allows only those workers who have been trained sufficiently, through demonstrating trade knowledge and practical craft-skills, to join our construction industry.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Alex Yam further asked if MOM conducts aptitude tests for construction workers.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: MOM complements the overseas testing by BCA with mandatory safety orientation training for all construction workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: The two-day mandatory Construction Safety Orientation Course (CSOC) equips workers with the relevant safety competencies and safety mindset to perform their duties and roles.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Melvin Yong expressed caution about the additional costs of all these amendments for businesses.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: For companies already complying with the existing WSH requirements, there should not be any additional costs incurred.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: However, and also rightfully so, these changes should spur errant companies to be more serious in their WSH efforts.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Every workplace accident exacts costs not only on the employer but also, importantly, on the workers and their families, a point that had been reiterated by quite a number of Members.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
